summary: Koichi Shinohara works in Buddhist studies, Sinology, and religious studies. He served as Professor at McMaster University (~1976–2004), coordinator of the Numata Program at the University of Toronto Mississauga (attested 2004), and Senior Lecturer at Yale University (~2004).

Specializing in Buddhist studies and Indology, Koichi Takahashi earned his PhD at the University of Tokyo by 2004 under Akira Saito and Yasunori Ejima. He held posts at the University of Tokyo as an assistant (attested 2005) and project researcher (attested 2015).

Koichi Yokoyama was a scholar of Buddhist studies and philosophy. He completed an MA at the University of Tokyo under Akira Hirakawa, also studying with Gyōin Hashimoto in 1970, and served as assistant professor at Rikkyo University (~1974–2003).
Koin Takada specialized in Buddhist studies, having studied at Ryukoku University (~1941–1944). A disciple of Gyōin Hashimoto, he succeeded him in 1967.

Koji Kamioka was an Iranian, Central Asian, and linguistics scholar. Educated at Kyoto University (~1957–1963) and under Yutaka Ochihara, he lectured at Kyoto Sangyo University in 1969 and served as assistant professor at Tokyo University of Foreign Studies (1972–2004).

Koji Takahashi was a Buddhist studies scholar who studied at Otani University and Bukkyo University, earning a doctorate in 1991. He served as assistant professor (~1964–2003) and professor (~1977–2003) at Bukkyo University, also editing for The Bukkyo Bunka Kenkyu.

Kojiro Yoshikawa was a Sinologist who studied at Kyoto University (~1923–1926). He served as Professor of Chinese Language and Literature at Kyoto University (~1947–1967) and president of Toho Gakkai (~1972–1980).

Kojun Fukui, a Buddhist studies and Sinology scholar, studied at Waseda University under Sokichi Tsuda. He became a professor at Waseda University (1941–1969) and served as president of Taisho University (1928–1968, 1972–1975).
Kojun Saito specialized in Indology and Buddhist studies. He studied under Seiren Matsunami and served as a lecturer at Taisho University (attested 1965).
Kokan Fujita is a Buddhist studies scholar who studied under Yujun Endo. He served as a professor at Koyasan University (attested 1995–2002).

Koken Sasaki was a scholar in Buddhist studies and Sinology who studied at Rissho University (~1950–1960). He held positions at Rissho University as assistant professor (~1970–1978), department chair (~1978–2002), and director/professor (~1998–2002).
Koki Kawagishi is a Buddhist studies scholar. In 1976, he was attested as a professor at both Eizan Gakuin and International Buddhist University.
Konchok Drakpa studied under Patrul Rinpoche and Jamgon Ju Mipham Gyatso, and later taught Dilgo Khyentse.
Konchok Gyatso is a Tibetologist who studied under Sherab Gyatso. He held an attested post at the Tibet Academy of Social Sciences in 2014.
Konchok Zangpo was a student of Patrul Rinpoche and Jamgon Ju Mipham Gyatso.

Konrad Klaus specializes in Indology and Tibetology. He studied at the University of Göttingen and the University of Marburg under Michael Hahn, served as interim professor at Bochum, Marburg, and Bonn (1999–2001), and succeeded Claus Vogel in 2001.

Kosaku Hamada was a scholar of Sinology, history, and archaeology. He studied at the University of Tokyo (~1901–1905), held a post there (~1909–1913), and later held a post at Kyoto University (~1917–1938).

Kosei Ishii specializes in Buddhist studies and philosophy. Educated at Waseda University under Akira Hirakawa, he held posts at Waseda, served as assistant professor at Komazawa Junior College (1994–2006), and was a professor and professor emeritus at Komazawa University.

Kosei Mizutani was a Buddhist studies scholar who studied at Ryukoku University and Bukkyo University. He served as assistant professor (~1957) and president (~1979–1989) of Bukkyo University, and was board chairman for Tokai Gakuen and Bukkyo Kyoiku Gakuen.

Kosei Tada was a Buddhist studies scholar who studied at the University of Tokyo. He held a post at Taisho University and served as board president of the Society for Buddhist Cultural Studies (attested 2004).
